newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong funds say Thai sell-off "nightmarish".
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong funds say Thai sell-off "nightmarish".

text.p: The continuing slide in Thai stocks on Monday prompted surprise and dismay among Asian fund managers based in Hong Kong.
Thailand's key stock index plummeted six percent on Monday, adding momentum to a 14-percent nose-dive over the past five trading sessions.
"For it to be down this much in five days is nightmarish," said Clive McDonnell, senior economist at Crosby Financial Holdings. "Obviously, there was pent-up selling pressure."

Traders and fund managers in Hong Kong said restrictions to foreign loans announced by the Bank of Thailand on Friday provided the catalyst for Monday's slump, pushing the SET index below the key 1,000 point barrier to a 37-month low of 944.63.
Regional traders, who allocate foreign funds around Asia, said foreigners sold across the board, unwinding long-term positions held in anticipation of a market bounce.

The loan restrictions were also considered a blow for Thailand's already weak economy. They place limits on short-term loans brought into the country by offshore banking units for relending to Thai clients, and are expected to eat into banks' margins, eroding earnings.

"Effectively this tightens money supply even further which means a slowing economy will get even slower," said one foreign fund manager. "Everybody's revising corporate earnings, GDP (gross domestic product), you name it, downwards."

Yet most experts were surprised by the violence of Monday's move. "I'm not quite sure what people expected -- (the Bank of Thailand has) been saying they were going to do this all along," said David Semple, regional strategist with Peregrine Investment in Hong Kong. "I'm taken aback that it's had such an impact on the market."
As recently as one month ago, foreign funds said they remained overweight in Thailand despite selling fuelled largely by weak domestic sentiment.
But on Monday foreign fund managers based in Hong Kong said most selling came from overseas institutions in the United States and Europe rather than Asian institutions.

Apart from Jardine Fleming Investment Management, which moved its model portfolio to an underweight position from overweight on Friday, most Asian fund managers said they were already out of the Thai market, having sold over the past two months.

While new foreign loan restrictions were blamed for Monday's sell-off, regional strategists said longer-term issues -- slowing growth, weak exports, a widening current account deficit and a volatile political landscape -- were at the root of the problem.

"I think the issues are really much deeper," said Abihijit Chakrabortti, regional strategist at Lehman Brothers in Hong Kong. "People have gotten very worried about the economy because people generally misread it."
A current account deficit of eight percent -- the worst in Southeast Asia -- is keeping interest rates and the cost of capital high.
"There is a real slowdown in the economy and quite a lot of pressure on the downside," Abihijit said.
